opus-5.5.text:
I think data is going to become increasingly central, and in some ways it's already the binding constraint people worry about most. If you look at the scaling laws, compute-optimal training says that as you grow your compute budget, you want to scale model size and the number of training tokens roughly in tandem. So every time compute goes up by, say, ten-fold, you need something like three times more data. Compute has been growing at around four to five times per year for frontier training runs, which means the appetite for data grows very quickly.

On the supply side, the stock of high-quality, human-generated public text is large but finite. When we at Epoch tried to estimate it, we found it's on the order of hundreds of trillions of tokens if you're generous about quality, and the largest training runs are already using a meaningful fraction of that. So if trends continue, we'd expect labs to more or less exhaust the readily available public text stock sometime in the latter half of this decade, give or take a few years depending on how aggressively you're willing to overtrain or repeat data.

Now, that doesn't mean progress stops. I think what changes is the *kind* of data that matters. A few things I'd expect:

First, multi-epoch training and better filtering buy you some time. Repeating data a few times seems to cost relatively little, so the effective stock is somewhat bigger than the raw count.

Second, other modalities: video, audio, images, and private or proprietary data. There's an enormous amount of that, though how much it transfers to the capabilities people care about, like reasoning, is still an open question.

Third, and I think most importantly, synthetic data and data generated through interaction. With reinforcement learning, self-play, and models generating and verifying their own reasoning traces, you're increasingly converting compute into data. In domains with good verifiers, like math and code, that loop can be quite powerful. So the line between "data" and "compute" starts to blur.

So my overall expectation is that raw human-written internet text becomes less of the story over time, and the question shifts to how efficiently you can turn compute into useful training signal. Data stays important, maybe more important than ever, but it becomes something you manufacture rather than something you scrape. And eventually, as AI systems get deployed in the economy, the data they gather from interacting with the real world could become a major source too, which matters for how these systems learn things that aren't written down anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response calls data a growing constraint overall, but does not say it may be the dominant factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It discusses high-quality public text and says how other data transfers to reasoning is an open question, but does not identify high-quality training data as a driver of current systems’ complex reasoning.

r003.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning with models generating and verifying reasoning traces, especially in math and code domains with verifiers, as a way to produce useful training signal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot at Epoch. I think the short answer is that data has been enormously important, and I expect it to remain important, but the nature of that importance is going to shift.

So if you look at the history of deep learning over the past decade or so, the big drivers of progress have been compute scaling, algorithmic improvements, and data. And data has been somewhat of a free ride, in a sense. The internet gave us this enormous corpus of human-generated text, and labs have been able to scale up their training datasets roughly in lockstep with compute, because the data was just there, waiting to be scraped. Our estimates suggest that the stock of high-quality public text is on the order of tens of trillions of tokens, maybe a few hundred trillion if you're generous about what counts as usable. And frontier training runs are now consuming a meaningful fraction of that. So at some point in the next several years, you can't just keep doubling the amount of natural text you train on, because it doesn't exist.

Now, I don't think that means progress stalls. What I think it means is that data stops being a passive input and becomes something labs actively produce and engineer. So you see this already with synthetic data, with models generating their own training signal, with verifiers and reward models that let you learn from outcomes rather than from human demonstrations. The reasoning models are a pretty clear example. A lot of the gains there come not from more internet text but from reinforcement learning on problems where you can check the answer, math, code, that sort of thing. In those domains, data is effectively a function of compute. You spend compute to generate attempts, you verify them, and you train on the ones that work.

So my expectation is that the bottleneck shifts from "how much data can we collect" to "how much data can we generate and how good is our signal for which generated data is useful." And that reframes the question somewhat. It makes data importance more entangled with compute and with algorithmic cleverness than it has been.

The caveat I'd add is that this works much better for some domains than others. It's easy to verify a proof or a unit test. It's much harder to verify whether a piece of long-horizon strategic advice was good, or whether a scientific hypothesis was fruitful. So I think there'll be an uneven frontier, where capabilities in verifiable domains race ahead and the ones that depend on scarce human judgment lag somewhat. Whether that gap closes depends on how good we get at building proxies for human judgment, and that's genuinely uncertain.

But if you're asking me to put a rough shape on it: I think over the next few years, natural data constraints will bite, and the response will be to substitute compute and better learning algorithms for raw data. And I'd expect that substitution to mostly succeed, so that data in the old sense becomes less of a binding constraint, even as the engineering of data becomes more central.

r001.rationale: The response says data remains important and that verifiable domains may advance faster, but it does not state that data may be the dominant factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies reinforcement learning on answer-checkable problems as a source of reasoning-model gains, using generated attempts that are verified and selected for training.

r003.rationale: It describes generating and verifying attempts for reinforcement learning, but does not specifically identify reasoning traces as the training material.

astra-6.text:
I expect data to become an increasingly important constraint on progress, particularly if we continue training models in roughly the way we do today. We can invest in more compute and build larger models, but getting more high-quality human-generated text is harder. There’s a finite stock of it, and that stock isn’t necessarily growing as quickly as the demand for training data.

But that doesn’t mean we simply hit a wall. It creates an incentive to use existing data more efficiently and to find other ways of generating useful training experience. That could include synthetic data, interactions with environments, or learning from feedback. In domains where you can check whether an answer is correct, a model can potentially generate examples and use that verification to improve.

So I’d distinguish the importance of human-generated data from the importance of learning experience more broadly. The former might become less central over time, while the latter remains crucial. The uncertainty is how effectively we can replace additional human data with experience that systems generate for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says data may increasingly constrain progress, but does not state that data may dominate capability gains for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies high-quality human text as valuable training data, but does not connect that data to the complex reasoning abilities of current AI systems.

r003.rationale: It mentions feedback and verification, but not reasoning traces used in reinforcement learning to train models toward correct-answer reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect data to become increasingly important as we use up the readily available sources of high-quality human-generated text. For a long time, you could improve models by putting more compute into training and increasing the amount of internet data they saw. That becomes harder to sustain if the supply of useful data doesn’t grow at the same rate as compute.

But I wouldn’t interpret that as a hard ceiling on progress. It changes the question to: how can we get more learning out of the data we have, and how can we generate new data? That could involve synthetic examples, interactions with an environment, or having models attempt tasks and receive feedback on whether they succeeded.

The crucial distinction is between generating more text and generating more useful information. A model producing answers and then training on those answers doesn’t automatically improve. You need some way to select or verify them. In domains where that’s possible, like mathematics or programming, computation can help produce valuable training data. So I’d expect data to become more of a constraint, while also expecting much more effort to go into making data better and generating it through computation.

r001.rationale: The response says data may become more of a constraint and mentions useful data for math or programming, but it does not say data may be the dominant factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It discusses high-quality text and useful training data, but does not connect them to the complex reasoning abilities of current AI systems.

r003.rationale: It mentions task attempts and feedback, but does not describe training with reasoning traces in reinforcement learning to produce reasoning that leads to correct answers.
